\chapter{Lo Siento}
\label{ch:spanish-sorry}
\hlchaptermodality{88}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can apologise in Spanish and choose between lo siento and perdón.}

Say lo siento for regret and perdón for fault or for catching someone's attention, hearing sentir — I feel it — inside the first and dōnāre — to give completely — inside the second.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[lo siento]{lo siento — \textquotedblleft{}I'm sorry,\textquotedblright{} i.e. \textquotedblleft{}I feel it\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C20-lo-siento}



\begin{quote}
You already know \textbf{por favor}, \textquotedblleft{}please.\textquotedblright{} The next courtesy phrase is \textbf{lo siento}. Spanish does not say \textquotedblleft{}I \emph{am} sorry\textquotedblright{} as an adjective; it says something closer to \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I feel this.\textquotedblright{}}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{lo} = \textquotedblleft{}it\textquotedblright{} — a \textbf{neuter} pronoun. It does not point at any noun; it points at the \textbf{situation itself}. Spanish keeps this one leftover neuter slot precisely for \textquotedblleft{}the whole business, unnamed.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{siento} = \textquotedblleft{}I feel,\textquotedblright{} from \textbf{sentir}, \textquotedblleft{}to feel,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \textbf{sentīre}. That root gave English a whole family: \textbf{sentiment}, \textbf{sense}, \textbf{consent} (\textquotedblleft{}feel together\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{resent} (\textquotedblleft{}feel back at\textquotedblright{}), and \textbf{sentence} (originally an \emph{opinion}, something felt).
\end{itemize}

So \textbf{lo siento} is literally \emph{\textquotedblleft{}I feel it.\textquotedblright{}} You are naming a feeling — regret, sympathy — rather than declaring a state about yourself. That is why it stretches so easily: \emph{lo siento mucho}, \textquotedblleft{}I feel it a lot,\textquotedblright{} works both for stepping on someone's foot and for hearing that their father died.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}siento\textquotedblright{} — I feel — then \textquotedblleft{}lo siento,\textquotedblright{} I feel it / I'm sorry
  \item \textquotedblleft{}lo siento mucho\textquotedblright{} — I'm so sorry
  \item \textquotedblleft{}siento\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}sentiment, sense, consent\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{lo siento} literally mean? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I feel it\textquotedblright{}} — \emph{siento}, \textquotedblleft{}I feel,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \emph{sentīre}.) What is the \emph{lo} pointing at? (The \textbf{situation}, not a noun — it is the neuter \textquotedblleft{}it.\textquotedblright{}) Next: Spanish's \emph{other} word for sorry, and when it is the right one.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[perdón]{perdón — the sorry that asks for something back}

\label{lesson:ES-C20-perdon}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Lo siento} names a feeling. Spanish keeps a \textbf{second} word for a different job — one that is not about your feelings at all, but about something you want from the other person.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{perdón} (\textquotedblleft{}pardon\textquotedblright{}), from the verb \textbf{perdonar} — Latin \textbf{per-} (\textquotedblleft{}thoroughly\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{dōnāre} (\textquotedblleft{}to give\textquotedblright{}). Literally: \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}to give completely.\textquotedblright{}}

That \emph{dōnāre} is English's \textbf{donate}, \textbf{donor}, and \textbf{condone}; the \emph{per-} is the same intensifier in \textbf{perfect} (\textquotedblleft{}thoroughly made\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{perturb}. So forgiveness, in Latin's picture of it, is a \textbf{gift given all the way} — you hand over the debt rather than keeping a share of it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The two are not interchangeable, and the difference follows straight from the etymologies:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{\textbf{lo siento}} & \textbf{\textbf{perdón}} \\
\midrule
literally & \textquotedblleft{}I feel it\textquotedblright{} & \textquotedblleft{}give {[}it{]} completely\textquotedblright{} \\
points at & \textbf{your} feeling & \textbf{their} forgiveness \\
use for & regret, sympathy & fault, or getting past someone \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \textbf{perdón} is what you say to squeeze through a crowd or catch a waiter's eye (English \textquotedblleft{}excuse me\textquotedblright{}), and to ask forgiveness for something \textbf{you did} — often stronger than \emph{lo siento}. \textbf{Lo siento} leans toward \textquotedblleft{}I'm sorry that happened,\textquotedblright{} including things that are nobody's fault at all.

Be honest about the edges: native speakers use whichever fits, the boundary is soft, and mixing them is not a real mistake — just a shade off.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}perdón\textquotedblright{} — pardon / excuse me
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}lo siento\textquotedblright{} for regret, \textquotedblleft{}perdón\textquotedblright{} for fault
  \item \textquotedblleft{}perdón\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}donate, condone\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{dōnāre} root
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do the two halves of \textbf{perdonar} mean? (\textbf{Per-}, \textquotedblleft{}thoroughly,\textquotedblright{} plus \textbf{dōnāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to give\textquotedblright{} — to give completely.) Which word do you use to get past someone in a corridor? (\textbf{Perdón}.) Which leans toward sympathy rather than fault? (\textbf{Lo siento} — \textquotedblleft{}I feel it.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
